question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the different types of choroidal neovascularization (CNV)?

options.D: Type 3 neovascularization originates in the capillary plexus of the retina and grown toward the RPE
options.C: Type 2 neovascularization typically appears as a area of red discoloration often associated with an exudate
options.B: Type 1 neovascularization occupies the compartment between the RPE and outer segments of the retina
options.A: Type 2 neovascularization is the most common form of CNV

explanation: The BCSC specifically indicates an anatomical classification for choroidal neovascularization: • Type 1 CNV o Occurs when new vessels from the choriocapillaris grow through a defect in the Bruch membrane into the sub-RPE space. o Leakage and bleeding can lead to the vascularized serous or fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment (PED). These fibrovascular PEDs often have an irregular contour. o Previously, known as "occult" CNV. o Poorly-delineated and stains late with irregular margins during fluorescein angiography. • Type 2 CNV o When abnormal vessels from the choriocapillaris penetrate through the RPE. Thus, type 2 CNV is located between the RPE and the outer segments of the retina. o Less common than type 1 CNV. o Has a lacy or gray-green appearance on fundus exam. o Previously, known as "classic" CNV. o Has a well-demarcated vascular pattern early on fluorescein angiography. The fluorescein dye then pools into the subneurosensory retinal space. • Type 3 CNV o Originates from blood vessels sprouting from the deep capillary plexus of the retina which grow downward toward the RPE. o Were originally called retinal angiomatous proliferations. o Appear as a small area of red discoloration frequently associated with an exudate. question: A 55-year old woman presented with an asymptomatic fundus lesion identified incidentally after cataract surgery in the left eye. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
explanation: Peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (PEHCR) is a peripheral (usually temporal) choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM). This entity is typically seen in the periphery of an older (mean: 77 years old) woman (69%) and is often asymptomatic. Approximately 25% of patients experience bilateral lesions. Treatment with anti-VEGF injections are sometimes recommended if exudation encroaches the macula. However, these lesions can often be observed as they are not sight-threatening in the same way as macular CNVMs. WRONG ANSWERS: • Choroidal melanoma would be the next most likely of the answer choices, but the presence of hard exudates on the edge closest to the macula makes this less likely, as melanomas rarely exude lipid. • Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments almost always cause symptoms of floaters or flashing lights. • Acute retinal necrosis typically presents with floaters, reduced vision, and pain. question: Which of the following is NOT considered to be a risk factor for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
explanation: Most population-based studies have found that the most important factor in developing age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is advanced age. In resource-rich countries, approximately 10% of individuals over the age of 65 years and 25% over the age of 75 years have AMD. Other classic risk factors: • Female • Cigarette smoking • Hypertension • Hypercholesterolemia • Positive family history • Cardiovascular disease • Light iris color • Caucasian race • Hyperopia The BCSC specifically mentions the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) study which found the prevalence of AMD to be highest in whites and lowest in African Americans. explanation: The OCT demonstrates prominent cystoid macular edema (CME). CME after cataract surgery is also known as Irvine-Gass syndrome. There are many causes for CME including vitreomacular traction, inflammation / uveitis, diabetes, X-linked hereditary retinoschisis, epiretinal membrane, and retinitis pigmentosa. Following cataract surgery the most important influences are inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins that disrupt blood vessel integrity resulting in leakage of fluid into the macula. Vitreomacular traction (VMT) can occur following vitreous loss during cataract surgery and can cause CME, but there is no evidence of VMT on this OCT. The first treatment for most cases of CME (including post-surgical CME) is medical therapy with topical steroids and topical NSAIDs. Q-Which of the following is generally FALSE regarding polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)?

question: Which of the following is generally FALSE regarding polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)?

options.D: fluorescein angiography (FA) is the optimal method of diagnosing PCV
options.C: The most frequent presentations of PCV are serous or hemorrhagic detachments of the retina and RPE
options.B: PCV lesions have a predilection to being located in the peripapillary region
options.A: PCV is classically described to occur in hypertensive middle-aged women of African or Asian ancestry

explanation: PCV was originally described by Yannuzzi et al in 1982 as a distinct form of choroidal neovascularization with a predilection for the peripapillary area. It is characterized by dilated choroidal vascular channels terminating in "polyps" leading to serous and hemorrhagic detachments of the retina and RPE. Another key feature is that there is either minimal or no cystic change of the overlying retina even if the subretinal hemorrhage is severe. Unlike choroidal neovascularization solely associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), PCV is classically associated with more darkly-pigmented individuals (e.g. Blacks and Asians). In fact, some experts believe that virtually all African American patients with neovascular AMD have concomitant PCV. In some clinical studies from Japan, over 50% of neovascular AMD patients had PCV. Also in contrast to neovascular AMD, PCV is not typically associated with drusen. explanation: The PHP is a visual field analyzer used specifically to detect new-onset neovascular AMD and to distinguish it from non-neovascular AMD. It is more sensitive than Amsler grid screening in detecting visual changes related to neovascular AMD. It uses the "Vernier acuity phenomenon" which is based on our ability to perceive a small difference in the spatial localization of two or more stimuli. This property permits the detection of early metamorphopsia caused by the displacement of photoreceptors by a choroidal neovascular membrane. Q-A 61-year-old female presents with the complaint of gradually reducing vision in the right eye for 6 months. She denies having any medical problems and does not take any medications. She has never had any eye surgeries, and until 6 months ago, was seeing "20/20." On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity is 20/60 OD. The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management option?

question: The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management option?

options.D: Pars Plana Vitrectomy with membrane peeling OD

explanation: The images depict an epiretinal membrane (ERM) with secondary cystoid macular edema (CME). Notice the prominent retinal striae on the color fundus photograph. A) Observation is inappropriate given that the patient is symptomatic and has moderately reduced vision. Since she has noticed worsening vision over the past 6 months, the vision is likely to continue deteriorating if observation is continued. B) Anti-VEGF therapy is inappropriate given that it has no efficacy for this condition. The CME is due to the circumfrential tractional forces exerted by the ERM on the retinal blood vessels running through the nerve fiber layer, and is not caused by inflammatory mediators. C) Topical or intravitreal steroids are inappropriate for this condition for the same reason as described for anti-VEGF therapy. D) Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling +/- internal limiting peeling is the appropriate option. Once the ERM is removed and the tractional forces are relieved, the CME resolves. Removing the internal limiting membrane along with the ERM will prevent recurrence of the ERM. An ERM is unable re-proliferate on the surface of the nerve fiber layer, which in part explains the popularity of internal limiting membrane peeling by vitreoretinal surgeons. explanation: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is characterized by the development of well-delineated serous retinal or RPE detachments. It typically occurs in young men and has some association with type A personalities and periods of high stress (although this relationship has never been proven). explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a poorly understood, idiopathic inflammatory condition of the inner choroid and/or outer retina. It tends to occur unilaterally in younger myopic females and often presents with central vision loss, enlarged blind spot, and photopsias. Photopsias are very characteristic of MEWDS and other poorly understood inflammatory conditions such as acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) and idiopathic enlarged blind spot syndrome; photopsias as a prominent feature in a young patient with central vision loss should raise suspicion for these conditions. The hallmark features of MEWDS are short-lived white dots usually lasting from days to a week after visual symptoms begin, macular pigment stippling, macular wreath- like punctuate hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and mild disc edema in some cases. With the advent of high quality spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) images, it has been discovered that there are non-specific but characteristic outer segment and RPE changes on SD-OCT. Essentially the OCT shows disruption of the usual contour of these layers without evidence of retinal edema. Similar changes can be seen in AZOOR, commotio retinae, and solar retinopathy. In the correct clinical context, however, the disruption of the normal inner segment- outer segment and RPE layers is essentially diagnostic of MEWDS. This is helpful in cases such as this question where the white dots have long since resolved by the time the patient is examined. On exam, his best corrected visual acuity in the left eye measures 20/100 and does not improve with pinhole. What in-office test can be performed to confirm the diagnosis?

question: What in-office test can be performed to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: As you may have guessed, all of the answers are eponymous tests from famous ophthalmologists. The patient’s symptoms and imaging data all indicate that he has a macular hole, specifically stage 3. The macular hole staging nomenclature adheres to the following parameters: • Stage 1 – also known as an impending macular hole, it demonstrates a loss of foveal depression without full thickness break. • Stage 2 – full thickness break ≤ 400 microns in diameter with the posterior hyaloid still attached to the fovea on OCT imaging. • Stage 3 – full thickness break > 400 microns with the posterior hyaloid noted to be detached over the macula; however, vitreous is still attached to the optic nerve head (thus, no posterior vitreous detachment observed on exam such as in our patient). • Stage 4 – same as stage 3 with the addition of a complete PVD. A full thickness macular hole can be difficult to discern from a partial thickness lamellar hole on fundus examination. If you do not have the luxury of OCT imaging, you can perform a Watze- Allen test (choice A) at the slit lamp. Using a 78D or 90D noncontact lens, a thin beam of light is projected over the macula across the fovea, and the patient is asked to report on its appearance. If the patient notices a break in the line, this may indicate a full thickness macular hole. The Jones test (choice B) is used to evaluate the lacrimal drainage system and is composed of two separate tests. The Jones I test investigates lacrimal outflow under normal physiologic conditions. The examiner places fluorescein into the conjunctival fornices and recovers it in the inferior nasal meatus by passing a cotton-tipped wire applicator into the region of the ostium of the nasolacrimal duct at 2 and 5 minutes. The Jones II test involves flushing residual fluorescein from the conjunctival sac using normal saline following an unsuccessful Jones I test to determine whether any reflux upon irrigation contains fluorescein in the retrieved fluid. There is no such thing as a Krimsky-Hirschberg test (choice C); however, there are separate Krimsky and Hirschberg tests. Both are used as screening tests to evaluate for the presence of strabismus. The Hirschberg test is performed by shining a light on the person’s eyes and observing where the light reflects off the corneas. In a person who is orthophoric, the light reflex lies slightly nasal from the center as a result of the cornea acting as a temporally-turned convex mirror to the observer. The light reflexes of both eyes are compared and should be symmetrical. Exotropia would demonstrate the corneal light reflex more nasally, and esotropia would show it more temporally. Similarily, hypertropia would demonstrate the reflex more inferiorly, and hypotropia would demonstrate it more superiorly. The Krimsky test employs the same principles as the Hirschberg test with the addition of prisms to quantify the amount of deviation by determining how much prism is required to re-center the reflex. The Marcus-Gunn test is typically how one checks for the presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (rAPD) in clinic. It is performed by shining a light into the left and right eyes rapidly and comparing pupillary constriction. A normal response would be equal constriction of both pupils regardless of which eye the light is directed at, indicating an intact direct and consensual pupillary light reflex. When the test is performed in an eye with a rAPD, light directed in the affected eye will cause only mild constriction of both pupils, while light in the unaffected eye will cause a normal constriction of both pupils. The key is to remember that rAPD is “relative”, thus if there is pathology affecting both pupillary light reflexes, then this test is no longer valid. Q-A 63-year-old male presents for evaluation of the left eye following pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) for an epiretinal membrane (ERM). Two weeks ago, the patient underwent PPV with membrane peeling and internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling. The patient's preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OS. The patient's best-corrected visual acuity is now 20/60 OS. The image depicts the patient's condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option at this time?

options.C: PPV with further ILM peeling and intraocular gas tamponade with face down positioning for 7 days

explanation: The images depict an eccentric full-thickness macular hole (FTMH) following PPV with ERM removal and ILM peeling. These holes occur in approximately 2% of cases following ERM removal. Putative mechanisms for hole formation include weakening of the glial structure of the retina induced by the decapitation of Müller cells, opening or de-roofing of intraretinal cysts, contraction of residual ILM, direct mechanical trauma, and ILM-staining dye toxicity. A) Observation is the most appropriate choice. An eccentric FTMH has minimal impact on the patient's subjective visual function unless it occurs either close to the fovea (within one disc diameter) or in the nasal macula within the papillomacular bundle. Furthermore, an eccentric FTMH does not seem to readily accumulate subretinal fluid with subsequent retinal detachment, though there may be a small risk of retinal detachment in highly myopic patients. The hole in this case is in the temporal macula and more than one disc diameter away from the fovea. The level of visual acuity is appropriate for a patient 2 weeks after ERM removal. B/C) It is inappropriate to subject this patient to an additional surgical procedure given that the FTMH will likely remain stable and asymptomatic indefinitely. It is evident from the images that both the ERM and ILM have been sufficiently removed from the central macula. D) Intravitreal ocriplasmin is inappropriate given that the posterior hyaloid has already been completely removed during the ERM removal (as evidenced by the images). explanation: Angioid streaks are breaks or irregularities in Bruch's membrane which can lead to: (1) spontaneous subretinal hemorrhages that are *not* necessarily related to choroidal neovascularization (CNV). explanation: The visual prognosis of central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is generally good, with >80% of affected eyes showing spontaneous resorption of fluid within 4 months. explanation: This vignette is alluding to the condition of ocular toxocariasis, which is a zoonotic infection caused by either Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati. Dogs and cats are the definitive hosts of these roundworms. These animals pass Toxocara eggs via their feces into the environment which are then ingested by humans (i.e. fecal-oral route of transmission). Common associations of transmission to humans include: sandboxes, playgrounds, kittens/puppies, pica eating disorder, and rarely undercooked meat. In humans, these organisms grow as larvae in the small intestine and then spread hematogenously via the portal circulation to various organs (e.g. eye, liver, heart, brain, muscle). Ocular toxocariasis is typically unilateral and presents most commonly via 1 of 3 presentations: • Peripheral granuloma o This can be associated with a fibrous brand that extends from the granuloma to a posterior location (e.g. optic disc or macula). • Posterior pole granuloma o This can lead to severe vision loss if the central macula is involved. • Panuveitis (moderate/severe) o This can mimic endogenous endophthalmitis. Any of these 3 common presentations can cause leukoria; thus ocular toxocariasis is in the differential diagnosis of retinoblastoma. One way of distinguishing ocular toxocariasis from retinoblastoma is the lack of calcium in the former condition. Since the ocular morbidity associated with this condition is thought to be due to the immune response against dead/dying larvae, systemic antihelminthic therapy is generally ineffective. Instead, local and systemic corticosteroids are the mainstays of treatment to reduce inflammation and its subsequent complications (e.g. macular edema). Systemic antihelminthic therapy (e.g. oral albendazole) may be considered if the larvae appear to be active, but steroids are still the mainstay of treatment. Oral albendazole is used in the treatment of visceral toxocariasis (fever, coughing, hepatomegaly, pneumonia, encephalitis) which rarely ever occurs simultaneously with ocular toxocariasis. Ocular toxocariasis is considered a clinical diagnosis; however, supportive laboratory tests that can be helpful include: antibody testing of ocular fluids or serums and/or recovering the actual larvae from vitrectomy specimens. explanation: There are two main groups of "hereditary hyaloideoretinopathies with optically empty vitreous" -- those with ocular signs exclusively and those with other systemic manifestations. Those with solely ocular signs include Jansen and Wagner disease. Those with other systemic signs include Stickler syndrome, "hereditary arthro-ophthalmopathy with stiff joints" (Weill-Marchesani variety), and variants with dwarfism. Stickler syndrome is the most common of these hyaloideoretinopathies. It is an autosomal dominant collagen disorder and the most commonly affected gene is COL2A1. Recall that type 2 collagen is present in vitreous, synovial fluid, and cartilage. Up to 60% of affected patients develop retinal detachments and 90% develop retinal tears due to premature vitreous breakdown, high myopia (>90%), and radial pigmented (perivascular) lattice degeneration. Prophylactic laser should be considered for extensive lattice, especially in high risk patients with a prior history of a retinal detachment in the fellow eye. Slit lamp examination will reveal abnormal vitreous that appears "optically empty" and liquefied. Subcortical cataracts can be seen. Stickler syndrome is often associated with systemic findings, such as facial abnormalities (e.g., Pierre Robin, cleft palate), joint hypermobility, hearing loss, and osteoarthritis. explanation: Rod monochromatism is an autosomal recessive inherited retinal disorder of the cone system leading to dysfunction of the cone photoreceptors. The disease is stationary and presents in infancy with nystagmus that may improve with age, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Visual acuity typically is worse than 20/100. There may be a paradoxical pupillary response (pupil constriction with transitioning from light to dark) and hyperopia is common. Some patients have an incomplete form with some cone function and residual color vision. Diagnosis is based on specialized color testing and ERG findings. Dark-adapted (DA) rod responses to a dim stimulus are normal, and to a bright stimulus can be normal or show mild attenuation of the a- and b-waves representing the loss of the cone system's contribution. However, photopic, light-adapted (LA) responses are typically completely undetectable from loss of the cone system. Fundus examination may be normal or show subtle granularity of the fovea, and this can be progressive. OCT of the foveola is often abnormal showing disruption of the ellipsoid zone, and a majority of patients have foveal hypoplasia. WRONG ANSWERS • (Choice A): Blue-cone monochromatism (BCM) is a stationary inherited disease of the cone system that results in selective loss the L ("red")- and M ("green")-cones but with preserved S ("blue")-cones. The condition can present similarly to rod monochromatism in infancy with nystagmus, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Unlikely rod monochromatism, BCM shows x-linked recessive inheritance, visual acuity is typically better (ranging from 20/80 to 20/200), and the majority of patients are myopic. Specialized color testing as well as ERG findings will further distinguish the two disorders. • (Choice B, C): Fundus albipunctatus and Oguchi disease are two congenital night-blinding disorders that have abnormal fundus findings. This is in contrast to congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) which has a normal fundus. All of these disorders are stationary inherited disorders of the rod system that present with nyctalopia. Fundus albipunctatus individuals show yellow-white dots that spare the fovea and extend into the midperiphery. It is due to mutations in the RDH5 gene which encodes an RPE protein necessary for rhodopsin regeneration leading to delayed rhodopsin regeneration in dark-adapted conditions. ERG responses demonstrate preserved cone function. ERG DA responses may normalize with extended dark adaptation due to the delayed rhodopsin regeneration. Oguchi disease has a peculiar fundus finding where the fundus appears normal after dark adaptation but develops a yellow sheen after brief light exposure, known as the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon). explanation: The congenital color deficiencies (deuteranopia, tritanopia, and protanopia) are *stationary* (non-progressive) in their color vision deficits. In addition, individuals with these conditions have normal visual acuity. These characteristics contrast with other forms of color blindness like cone dystrophy. explanation: Best disease is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the VMD2 gene (aka as the BEST 1 gene). This gene encodes the protein, "bestrophin", which is a transmembrane chloride channel located in the basolateral membrane of the RPE. Individuals with Best disease show a yellow, yolk-like (vitelliform) macular lesion in childhood which eventually breaks down into an atrophic appearance (i.e. "scrambled egg yolk"). Despite the prominent appearance of the macular lesion, these individuals surprisingly maintain good visual acuity in the majority of the cases. Approximately 20% of these patients will develop a choroidal neovascular membrane which reduces vision to the 20/200 level. Another pearl to remember about Best disease is that the ERG is typically normal while the EOG is always abnormal (i.e. Arden ratio < 1.5).
